limitations_and_boundaries: GNNs are at most as powerful as the WL test in distinguishing graph structures.
The analysis is limited to the neighborhood aggregation (message passing) framework.
Theoretical results do not directly address generalization ability.

On some datasets, GNN training accuracies never exceed those of the WL subtree kernel, indicating an upper bound on representational capacity.

methods.name: GIN (Graph Isomorphism Network)
methods.protocol_description: GIN uses sum aggregation followed by an MLP. Two variants: GIN-0 (epsilon fixed to 0) and GIN-epsilon (epsilon learned). 5 GNN layers, 2-layer MLPs, batch normalization, Adam optimizer with initial lr 0.01 decayed by 0.5 every 50 epochs. Hyperparameters tuned: hidden units (16,32 for bio; 64 for social), batch size (32,128), dropout (0,0.5), number of epochs selected by best cross-validation accuracy.

methods.name: GNN variants (mean/max/sum aggregators, 1-layer/MLP)
methods.protocol_description: Variants include mean-1-layer (GCN), max-1-layer (GraphSAGE), sum-1-layer, mean-MLP, max-MLP. Same architecture and hyperparameter settings as GIN for fair comparison.

methods.name: WL subtree kernel
methods.protocol_description: WL subtree kernel with C-SVM classifier. Hyperparameters tuned: C of SVM, number of WL iterations (1-6).

methods.name: Theoretical framework based on WL test and multisets
methods.protocol_description: The framework represents neighbor feature vectors as a multiset and analyzes the injectivity of aggregation functions. A GNN is as powerful as the WL test if its aggregation and readout functions are injective.
